title: Boot or Logon Autostart Execution: Time Providers
shortTitle: Boot or Logon Autostart Execution: Time Providers
summary: The Windows Time service, W32Time, keeps clocks aligned across and within a domain, and it does the work through time provider libraries that read timestamps from network or hardware sources and publish them to clients. Each provider is registered in its own subkey under the TimeProviders key of the time service, where a library name value points at the module and an enabled value decides whether it runs. The provider manager, directed by the service control manager, loads and starts the listed providers at system startup and whenever the configuration changes. An adversary with administrator rights creates a new subkey whose library value points at their own module, which is loaded at every boot; because the service runs as the Local Service account, the code starts reliably but with limited rights, and is generally a stepping stone rather than a full compromise. The artefacts are new subkeys under the time provider key, an unsigned module loaded by the time service, and module paths outside the system directory. A default host carries a very small known set of providers, so an unfamiliar provider name is the discriminator.

beginner.definition: This technique uses the Windows Time service to start an attacker's library at boot. That service keeps the computer clock correct, and it uses small helper libraries called time providers. Each provider is listed in its own registry subkey. An attacker creates a new subkey that points to their own library. The service then loads that library every time the computer starts. This sub-technique differs from its parent because the system start, and not a user sign in, sets off the code.
beginner.whyItMatters: Time settings are boring and rarely reviewed, so an extra provider is easy to miss. The registry change survives restarts and needs no scheduled task or login script. The attacker's library runs inside a service, which people tend to trust more than a file in a user folder. If you never check the provider list, this kind of entry can sit on the machine for a very long time.
howItWorks: Windows keeps the computer clock correct with a service called the Windows Time service.
That service uses helper libraries, called time providers, to read time from the network or hardware.
Each provider is registered in its own registry subkey under the time provider key.
An attacker creates a new subkey whose library value points to their own file.
At boot, or when the settings change, the service loads the library and runs the attacker's code.
The code runs as the Local Service account, so it starts reliably but with limited rights.
beginner.example: Think of a railway station where every clock is set by a small plug-in device. The station office keeps a drawer of approved devices, and each one has a card on the wall. At opening time a clerk fits every device that has a card. If someone adds a card for their own device, the clerk fits it every morning, and the device can quietly do other work while it pretends to tell the time.
takeaways: Time providers are libraries registered under the Windows Time service.
One new registry subkey makes the service load an attacker's library at every boot.
The code runs as the Local Service account, so expect limited rights but real persistence.

objectives: Explain what the Windows Time service does and why it uses providers.
Describe how time providers are registered and started.
Identify the registry key and the values involved in this technique.
Explain the rights held by the account that runs provider code.
Detect an unsigned module loaded by the time service.
Compare the default provider set with an unexpected addition.
